Mitigation of AC Induced Voltage on Buried Metallic Pipelines.
Electrical currents and electromagnetic fields from the powerline in close proximity of a pipeline can produce AC voltages on pipelines. These can vary and are difficult  to predict.
Clear Right-of-Ways are difficult to obtain for new pipelines and they usually share an existing ROW with overhead electric power transmission systems.
This present issues in safety, as induced voltage can provide shock hazards to personnel safety, and pipeline integrity, like coating damage and AC induced corrosion.
Safety standards for personnel are based on Touch and Step potentials, which can result in shock and hazards.
North American standards are regulated by NACE RP0177, which requires voltages above 15 volts to be mitigated, and ANSI/IEEE 80, which provides safety criteria related to heart fibrillation.
Coating damage can occur when voltage exceeds the dielectric strength of the coating.
AC induced corrosion is primarily a function of current density on steel structures.
Visual examples of AC induces corrosion.
AC induced voltages on a pipeline usually occur by capacitative, resistive or inductive coupling.
Capacitive coupling is caused by the accumulation of electrostatic charge, usually during construction. It is unlikely on buried pipelines.
Resistive coupling is caused by unbalanced phase to phase or phase to ground faults. It usually occurs during abnormal operating conditions.
Inductive coupling happens when a current flow in the powerline creates an electromagnetic field surrounding the conductors. It occurs during normal operating conditions of the powerline.
Some factors that contribute to AC interference are soil resistivity values, powerline characteristics and pipeline coating.
AC interference mitigation includes parallel zinc ribbons, non-metallic casing vents and equipotential gradient control mats.

Defenition of AC Interference: it occurs when electrical currents and electromagnetic fields from nearby power lines induce unpredictable voltages on pipelines.
Due to limited space, new pipelines often share Right-of-Way (ROW) corridors with existing overhead power transmission lines.
Induced AC in shared ROWs poses safety risks to personnel and pipeline integrity.
Personnel safety is at risk due to shock hazards from step and touch potentials, which arise from voltage differences between the ground and nearby structures.
Illustrations of touch and step potentials.
North American standards define thresholds for AC step voltages and establish safety limits to prevent shock and heart fibrillation risks, based on factors like duration and surface resistivity.
High fault currents can discharge through coating defects, potentially damaging pipeline coatings and causing arching stress.
AC-induced corrosion on steel pipelines depends on current density, with risks increasing above 30 A/m2, and becoming severe beyond 100 A/m2.
Visual examples of AC induced corrosion.
Three mechanisms of AC interference.
Capacitive coupling happens when electric charge builds up between power lines and nearby ungrounded pipelines, causing induced voltages.
Resistive coupling (electrolytic) occurs when fault currents from power lines flow through the ground and into nearby buried metal structures.
Inductive coupling occurs when electromagnetic fields from power lines induce AC voltages on nearby pipelines, even under normal operating conditions.

Part 1: Introduction and Basics.
Negotiations focus on reducing or binding tariffs, and abolishing NTBs. All member-coutries did not participate in the first seven rounds.
The main focus is lowering the tariffs, hence the limit progress in QRs and NTBs. The Uruguay Rounds had the most comprehensive negotiations.

Negotiations have been conducted in a selective product-by-product approach until 1961. Subsequent rounds used reduction formulas. After the Uruguay Round, Information Technology Agreement and Pharmaceuticals were introduced.
There are two formulas for tariff reduction: tariff-independent reduction modalities and tariff-dependent reduction formulas. One relevant formula is the 'Swiss Formula'.
A chart illustrates the difference between initial tariff, 50% linear cut and Swiss Formula cut.
After eight rounds of negotiations, unfinished business remains in NAMA. Tariffs are an important source of distortions and economic costs.
There is continued bias in protection against developing countries through tariff peaks and escalation.
Part 2: From Doha to July Framework via Cancun.
The Doha Ministerial negotiations aim to reduce or eliminate tariffs, tariff peaks and escalation, and reducing non-tariff barriers, especially for developing countries.

Negotiations take into account special needs and interests of developing countries through reduction commitments,
in accordance with
Article XXVIII bis of GATT 1994, and as per paragraph 50 of the Doha Declaration.
NAMA starts in January 2002 and, after several delays, is to be concluded by the end of 2006.
The July framework contains the initial elements of future work on modalities, tariff reduction and elimination, and sectoral initiatives, among others.
Part 3: Run-up to Hong Kong and Outcome of Hong Kong Ministerial.
The USA suggested a simple Swiss formula with two coefficients, a higher coefficient for developing countries, and sectoral negotiations based on critical mass.
ABI suggested a Swiss formula based on national duty, Caribbean countries proposed a development oriented tariff reduction.
There is growing support for a Simple Swiss formula with dual coefficients. Pakistan proposed a compromise formula with two coefficients.
EU proposed higher coefficients for developing countries and advocated for a simple Swiss formula. For advanced developing countries, EU proposed a tariff cap of 15%.

The outcome was: commitment to Doha Mandate and July Framework, Swiss formula with multiple coefficients, reduction/elimination of tariff peaks and escalation, sectoral initiatives being non-mandatory.
Part 4: Select Issues and Implications.
The sectoral discussion focused on product coverage, critical mass, final target rates and options for S&D. There is no clarity on the multilaterization of sectoral outcome.
The reaffirmed importance of S&D treatment and reciprocity is positive but operationalization of LTFR was not clarified and there is controversy regarding flexibilities.
LDCs are exempted from formula tariff reduction and there was no progress on deciding the elements of the flexibilities.
Positions are polarized, the number of products and members is limited, there is strong evidence of under-utilization and seeking solutions within trade negotiations may be counter-productive.
Conflicting positions include conflicting interests among developing countries and LDCs.
The Indian industry position is NOT uniform.
The key to a successful negotiation is conflict resolution and convergence of positions.

This is a workshop on WTO-related issues for government officials from the SAARC region, conducted by Manab Majumdar.
The topic of Non-Agricultural Market Access (NAMA)

The core tools used for negotiations on NAMA are aimed to, Reduction of tariffs,
Binding of tariffs, and 
Reduction/abolition of NTBs. Earlier negotiation rounds had limited participation and mostly focused on tariff cuts. The Uruguay Round was the first to include all members and address the issues.

NAMA remains unfinished, with tariff peaks and escalation continuing to distort trade and effecting  developing country exports, tackling these is importand for development. The Doha Ministerial put this issue on the negotiating agenda.

The Doha Ministerial mandated NAMA negotiations to reduce or eliminate tariffs, tariff peaks, high tariffs, tariff escalation, and non-tariff barriers, especially on products of export interest to developing countries.

The July Framework on NAMA proposes applying a non-linear formula for tariff reductions, ensuring greater  cuts for higher tariffs on a line-by-line basis. It also grants developing countries flexibility through the principle of less than full reciprocity.

The Hong Kong Ministerial reaffirmed commitment to the Doha Mandate and elements of the July Framework. It adopted the Swiss formula with (multiple) coefficients, retained less than full reciprocity. Sectoral initiatives were made non-mandatory, and the deadline to set up modalities by 30 April was missed.

HKMCinstructed identification of sectors with potential for sufficient participation. Discussions focused on product coverage, critical mass, final target rates, and options for Special and Differential (S&D).

The HKMC called for intensified work on assessing preference erosion, but positions remain extremely polarized with no consensus. Seeking solutions within negotiations may be counter productive,  an adjustment mechanism outside WTO could be more effective.

When talking about the transfer of heat energy, one form is radiation.
Radiation can travel through a vacuum, like the light from the Sun does.
Another form of energy transfer is conduction.
In this case, heat transfers through matter.
The third form is convection, which typically includes the movement of air.
Hot air rises, which means energy is also moving.
Another example of radiation would be a campfire.
In conduction the energy is transferred from one substance to another or within a substance and is particularly effective in metals.
Conduction does not work well with air. Air is an insulator.
Convection happens in a fluid, like air or water.
It happens in formations like clouds.
The surface of the Earth being hot and the atmosphere getting colder father away from the Earth has a huge impact on the movement of air.
One way to measure the heat in the atmosphere is a thermometer.
The design of a thermometer can vary but the principle is always the same.
There are three main scales to measure temperature: Fahrenheit, Celsius and Kelvin.
Fahrenheit is the scale used in the US.
The rest of the world typically uses Celsius.
The Kelvin scale is based on a concept know as absolute zero.
The term inversion comes from the change in the way the layers of air warm up or cool down.

Forums were cultural centers of Roman cities, usually located at the intersection of the Cardo Maximus and Decumanus.
Religious buildings, such as temples, were modeled after Greek designs.
Spectacle buildings, like theaters, were similar to Greek theaters.
The design of the amphitheater was based on the fusion of two theaters.
One example is the Colosseum which was built in 8 years and was 160 feet tall.
The velarium was a retractable awning that shaded spectators from the sun and was operated by members of the Roman navy.
The circus was a racetrack used for horse and quadriga competitions.
Arches were built to commemorate Roman victories or honor military generals.
Commemorative columns were decorated with relief sculptures, some depicting historical events, and were built to honor individuals.
Insulae were urban apartment buildings in Roman cities.
Buildings upto 4 floors high were contructed.
Domus were typically residences for important or wealthy individuals in each Roman city.
Villas were houses located outside cities, used either for agricultural purposes or as country homes for wealthy and important individuals.
The palaces were the residence of the emperor.

Victor Leung presents his project about Prototyping Non-Developable Paper Models without Glueing Tabs.
Papercraft is a type of craft that consists of creating shapes by cutting, folding, and glueing pieces of paper.
In design, paper models are used to represent buildings.
Some of the non-developable surfaces used in design are so thin that it becomes incredibly difficult to recreate them on a smaller scale.
Paper is frequently used to model these complex architectural surfaces.
The limitations of paper as a material are not compatible with non-developable surfaces.
The first step in recreating non-developable surfaces with paper is to create an approximation consisting of flat elements.
The most dominant technique is planar mesh.
The second step of the process is to decide how to cut the planes apart.
Cutting all planes separately leads to needing a lot of glueing. A common solution is to link some of the planes together.
Although this method is usually helpful, the strips can overlap in some cases.
The current methods include glueing tabs. These make the assembling process tedious since it is necessary to apply only the right amount of glue to each tab.
Additionally, it is necessary to apply pressure to the drying tabs, which slows down the glueing process.
Victor proposes a new approach that introduces changes to the segmentation process and eliminates the need for glue.
His method uses two sets of segmentation results.
The use of parallel strips, in particular the orange peel method, is more fitting than the tree light strips for this new approach.
Aesthetically, this new method avoids glueing tabs and allows for both sides of the surface to be smooth.
It also allows for the laser burn cutting marks to be hidden between the two layers of paper.
The glueing process is significantly faster as it is now possible to apply the glue as a spray or with a roller.
Drying time is also eliminated.
Adding a second layer to the structure makes the model stronger.
To use this model with thicker materials, it is possible to offset the mesh model to compensate the edges.
For regular triangular or square tessellations, a precompiled solution can be used.
This new proposal is a low cost method for building large models.
Apart from the laser cutter, there are no special tools needed.
Textures can be easily printed onto the paper before cutting.

Victor Leung, an independent researcher and MIT graduate, is here to present his talk on 'Prototyping Non-Developable Paper Models Without Gluing Tabs.
Victor introduces the topic by saying it's about creating beautiful paper models.
In the context of architectural design, paper models have long been used to represent buildings and are often seen as an important tool in the design process.
Victor talks about how the limitations of paper prevent the creation of non-developable surfaces.
Victor explains that for complex non-developable surfaces, the first step is to create an approximation composed of flat elements.
The second step is to decide how to cut it apart.
The goal is to create as few gluing edges as possible.
The assembly process is tedious and requires precise amounts of glue.
Victor mentions that there are problems, but there has been little innovation to improve the process.
Victor Leung proposes a new method for the meshing and segmentation steps, as well as the assembly of paper models, so that they no longer require gluing tabs.
Victor says they introduced a second layer of paper strips, which is a new element in his method.
Victor explains that the double-layer approach has advantages, such as hiding the gluing tabs, which improves the model's aesthetics.
This new two layer structure eliminates the stepping art effect on the model.
The previously tedious manual assembly process is now much easier, as adhesive can be applied to the underside of each layer using spray or a roller.
When using this method there is really no limitations on the size of the models.
Concluding the presentation, Victor states that another benefit of this model is the ability to achieve double sided textures more easily, as they can be printed on two separate sheets of paper.

Meigs Field Airport was built on Northerly Island, a location first proposed by urban planner Daniel Burnham in the early 1900s. Construction was delayed for decades due to the Great Depression and World War II. The airport finally opened in 1948 and quickly became the busiest airport in the US, a vital hub for transportation in Chicago.

During the 80s, Meigs Field reached its peakoperational, handling up to 80,000 landings a year. It served a wide range of purposes: corporate travel, emergency medical flights, VIP transport, and later, flight training. However, traffic began to decline due to increased landing fees and political pressure to repurpose the land.

On March 30, 2003, without warning, Mayor Daley ordered crews to destroy the airport’s runway overnight by carving giant X’s into the runways pavement. Citing post-9/11 security concerns, Daley bypassed the FAA and sparked a legal battle. The FAA later fined the city, and in 2006, Chicago officially paid the penalty. The former airport land is now a park and concert venue.

Eddie talks about one strong part of the film Charles McGraw’s role as Red Kluger, which helped him become known in the industry for more than just small roles.

The film was made during a troubled time when Howard Hughes was in charge of RKO. His poor leadership almost ruined the studio, just like he crashed his test plane, the XF-11, on its first flight over Los Angeles.

The real creative force behind the film was director Felix Feist, who likely had a strong hand in the screenplay. He had earlier directed The Devil Thumbs a Ride for RKO, and The Threat closely follows the same plot, about a violent criminal holding innocent people hostage.

Before The Threat, McGraw had appeared in many films with top directors like Robert Siodmak and Anthony Mann. Here, he steps out of the background to take center stage a fierce presence unleashed by director Felix Feist on a worn down supporting cast, including Michael O'Shea, Frank Conroy, Don McGuire, and Virginia Grey.

The actress was always petite, but in this film, she appeared especially thin and frail, possibly due to personal struggles. Virginia Grey had been romantically involved with Clark Gable after the death of his wife, Carole Lombard, in 1942.
Top billed Michael O'Shea was seen as a lower budget version of Jimmy Cagney. Although he was expected to become a big star, true stardom never came his way.

McGuire went on to have a successful career as a writer and director in the 1950s, working with Jerry Lewis and Frank Sinatra, both of whom became close friends. Later in life, he earned an Oscar nomination for his role in creating the 1982 hit Tootsie.

A simplicial k-chain is a formal sum of k-dimensional simplices in a simplicial complex KK. These chains are algebraic representations of geometric objects, such as points, edges, triangles, etc., and form the basis for computing homology

Defines the boundary operator, which maps a k-simplex to a sum of its (k−1)-dimensional faces. Key property: boundaries have no boundaries, i.e., applying the boundary operator twice yields zero. This is central in identifying cycles and boundaries

Defines the homology group as the quotient group 
Hk(K) = Zk(K)/Bk(K)
where:
Zk(K) is the group of k-cycles (chains with zero boundary),
Bk(K) is the group of k-boundaries (boundaries of (k+1)-chains).
Homology captures essential topological features like holes and voids

Explains that Delaunay triangulation is a method for connecting a set of points into triangles such that no point lies inside the circumcircle of any triangle, assuming the points are in general position
Describes persistence as the difference between the scale when a cycle appears and when it disappears, indicating the feature’s significance

Homology classifies objects by connectivity and n-dimensional holes.
